title: Every field has a visible, persistent label
statement: Each input has a visible text label that stays visible while typing; placeholders are not used as the only label.
rationale: Maps to: Nielsen #6; WCAG 3.3.2. Placeholder-only labels disappear on input, burden memory, look like pre-filled values, often fail contrast, and are unreliable for assistive tech.
audit_check: Does every input have a visible label that remains after the user starts typing?
citation: Sherwin, K. (2014). Placeholders in Form Fields Are Harmful. NN/g; WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.2, 1.3.1, 2.5.3.

title: Labels above fields for fastest completion
statement: Place labels above inputs (top-aligned) in single-column forms; left-aligned labels only when scanning label names matters more than speed.
rationale: Maps to: Gestalt proximity. Eye-tracking showed top-aligned labels yield the fastest completion with fewest fixations; they also work on mobile and with long translations.
audit_check: Are labels top-aligned and close to their fields?
citation: Penzo, M. (2006). Label Placement in Forms. UXmatters; Wroblewski, L. (2008). Web Form Design. Rosenfeld Media.

title: Use a single-column layout
statement: Arrange form fields in one column, except closely related short fields (e.g., city/postcode) that can share a row.
rationale: Maps to: Nielsen #8. Multi-column forms cause users to skip fields or misinterpret the reading order, and break on narrow screens.
audit_check: Is the form laid out in a single column?
citation: Baymard Institute checkout research; Jarrett, C. & Gaffney, G. (2009). Forms that Work. Morgan Kaufmann.

title: Validate inline after the field is completed
statement: Validate fields when the user leaves them (on blur) or after a short pause for complex inputs; do not validate while users are still typing their first attempt, and do not wait until submit for everything.
rationale: Maps to: Nielsen #9; WCAG 3.3.1, 3.3.3. In a 2009 test, inline validation produced a 22% increase in success, 22% fewer errors, 31% higher satisfaction, 42% faster completion and 47% fewer eye fixations versus after-submit validation.
audit_check: Are errors shown next to the field after it is completed (not only after submit, and not prematurely while typing)?
citation: Wroblewski, L. (2009). Inline Validation in Web Forms. A List Apart.

title: Show an error summary and inline messages on submit
statement: On submit with errors, show an error summary at the top linking to each field, move focus to it, and show a specific message next to each field.
rationale: Maps to: Nielsen #9; WCAG 3.3.1. Users of all abilities, including screen reader users, need to know errors exist and get to them quickly.
audit_check: On failed submit, is there an error summary with links to each field, and specific inline messages?
citation: GOV.UK Design System: Error summary & Error message components; WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.1, 3.3.3.

title: Error messages are specific and constructive
statement: Error messages say exactly what is wrong and how to fix it, in plain language, without blaming the user (e.g., "Enter a date of birth in the past" not "Invalid input").
rationale: Maps to: Nielsen #9. Vague errors increase recovery time and abandonment.
audit_check: Do error messages name the field, describe the problem and the fix?
citation: Nielsen, J. (2001). Error Message Guidelines. NN/g; GOV.UK Design System: Error message.

title: Preserve user input after errors and navigation
statement: Never clear valid fields after a validation error, page reload or back navigation (except sensitive fields like passwords/CVV where required).
rationale: Maps to: Nielsen #3; WCAG 3.3.7. Re-entering data is a major cause of frustration and abandonment.
audit_check: After a failed submit or going back, are previously entered values still present?

title: Do not ask for the same information twice
statement: Auto-fill or offer to reuse information already given in the same process (e.g., "billing same as shipping").
rationale: Maps to: WCAG 3.3.7. Redundant entry adds effort and errors and is a WCAG 2.2 Level A requirement.
audit_check: Is any information requested more than once in a flow?

title: Ask only for what you need
statement: Every field must be justified by a clear need; remove optional and nice-to-have fields, or defer them until after the core task.
rationale: Maps to: Nielsen #8. Each extra field increases effort and abandonment; unnecessary personal data collection also conflicts with data minimisation (GDPR Art. 5).
audit_check: Is every field necessary for the task at this point?

title: Clearly mark optional (or required) fields
statement: Mark optional fields with "(optional)" when most fields are required, or mark required fields consistently; explain any symbol used.
rationale: Maps to: Nielsen #6. Users otherwise guess and either skip required fields or waste effort on optional ones.
audit_check: Is it clear which fields are optional or required?

title: Use appropriate input types and mobile keyboards
statement: Use type="email", "tel", "url", "number" (or inputmode="numeric" for codes), and date controls appropriately so mobile users get the right keyboard.
rationale: Maps to: Nielsen #7. Correct keyboards reduce typing errors and effort on touch devices.
audit_check: Do fields trigger the appropriate mobile keyboard?

title: Support browser autofill with autocomplete attributes
statement: Add correct autocomplete tokens (name, email, tel, street-address, postal-code, cc-number, one-time-code, new-password, current-password).
rationale: Maps to: WCAG 1.3.5. Autofill speeds completion dramatically and is required for personal data fields under WCAG 1.3.5.
audit_check: Do personal-data fields have valid autocomplete attributes?

title: Size fields to the expected input length
statement: Make field widths reflect the expected length (short for postcode/CVV, long for address lines).

audit_check: Do field widths match expected input length?

title: Accept input in any reasonable format
statement: Accept spaces, dashes, brackets, mixed case and leading/trailing spaces in phone numbers, card numbers, postcodes and codes; normalize on the server.
rationale: Maps to: Nielsen #5. Strict format rules create avoidable errors (Postel’s law).

title: Use radios for few options and autocomplete for many
statement: Use radio buttons for up to about 5–7 mutually exclusive options so all are visible; use a select for longer lists, and an autocomplete/combobox for very long lists such as countries.
rationale: Maps to: Nielsen #6. Dropdowns hide options and require extra clicks; long dropdowns are hard to scan.

title: Use the right date input for the date type
statement: For memorable dates (date of birth), use separate day/month/year text inputs; for nearby dates, a date picker can help; always show the expected format.
rationale: Maps to: Nielsen #5. Date pickers are slow for distant dates; ambiguous formats cause errors across locales.
audit_check: Is the date input appropriate to the kind of date and is the format clear?

statement: Keep the primary submit button enabled and explain errors on submit, instead of disabling it until the form is valid.

statement: Primary buttons use specific verbs ("Create account", "Pay £24.99") rather than generic labels ("Submit", "OK").

title: Password fields support managers, paste and visibility
statement: Allow paste and password managers, offer a show/hide toggle, show requirements before typing, and do not impose composition rules or periodic changes.

statement: Use a single "Full name" field unless separate parts are really needed; accept apostrophes, hyphens, spaces, accents and non-Latin characters; do not require a last name.

statement: For limited text fields, show the limit and remaining characters; do not silently truncate.

statement: Never pre-check boxes for marketing, data sharing, terms acceptance or paid extras.

audit_check: Is "Reject all" as easy and visible as "Accept all"?

title: Explain data use at the point of collection
statement: Explain why personal data is needed and how it will be used right where it is requested.
rationale: Maps to: GDPR. Transparency builds trust and is required by GDPR Art. 13.
audit_check: Is the purpose of personal data requests explained in context?

title: No deceptive patterns
statement: The interface must not use fake urgency, fake scarcity, confirmshaming, sneaking, preselection, nagging, obstruction or disguised ads.
rationale: Maps to: Ethics. Deceptive patterns harm users and are increasingly illegal.
audit_check: Is the interface free of known deceptive patterns? (see dark pattern taxonomy)

title: Everything works with a keyboard
statement: All functionality is operable by keyboard with a logical focus order and no keyboard traps.
rationale: Maps to: WCAG 2.1.1. Essential for keyboard, switch and screen reader users.
audit_check: Can all functionality be reached and operated by keyboard in a logical order?

title: Focus is always visible and not obscured
statement: Keyboard focus has a clearly visible indicator and is not hidden behind sticky headers, cookie banners or chat widgets.
rationale: Maps to: WCAG 2.4.7. Users must see where they are.
audit_check: Is focus clearly visible and never fully hidden?

title: Controls have accessible names
statement: Buttons, links, inputs, icons and frames have programmatic names that match visible labels.
rationale: Maps to: WCAG 4.1.2. Screen reader and voice control users depend on names.
audit_check: Do all interactive elements and iframes have accessible names matching visible labels?

title: Modals manage focus correctly
statement: Opening a dialog moves focus into it, traps focus while open, closes with Escape, and returns focus to the trigger on close.
rationale: Maps to: WCAG 2.4.3. Otherwise keyboard and screen reader users get lost.
audit_check: Do dialogs move, contain and restore focus, and close with Escape?

title: Respect reduced-motion preferences
statement: Honor prefers-reduced-motion; avoid parallax and large motion triggered by interaction, or allow disabling it.
rationale: Maps to: WCAG 2.3.3. Motion can cause vestibular disorders symptoms.
audit_check: Does the site honor prefers-reduced-motion and avoid non-essential motion?

title: Video has captions and audio has transcripts
statement: Provide captions for prerecorded video with audio, transcripts for audio, and audio description where needed.
rationale: Maps to: WCAG 1.2.2. Deaf and hard-of-hearing users, and users in sound-off contexts, need captions.
audit_check: Do videos have accurate captions?

title: Page language is declared
statement: Set the lang attribute on html and on passages in other languages.
rationale: Maps to: WCAG 3.1.1. Screen readers need it to pronounce correctly.
audit_check: Is the page language declared?

title: Publish an accessibility statement
statement: Provide an accessibility statement with conformance status, known issues and contact for feedback.

title: Disclose AI involvement
statement: Clearly indicate when content or responses are AI-generated and when users are talking to a bot.

title: Set expectations about capabilities and limits
statement: Explain what the AI can and cannot do and how accurate it is likely to be, with examples of good requests.
rationale: Maps to: HAX G1–G2. Mismatched expectations cause misuse and distrust.
audit_check: Does the AI feature explain its capabilities and limitations?

title: Show sources and confidence for AI outputs
statement: Cite sources for factual claims, show uncertainty, and make verification easy.
rationale: Maps to: HAX G11. Counters automation bias and hallucination risk.
audit_check: Do AI answers show sources or confidence so users can verify?
citation: Amershi et al. (2019) G11; Parasuraman & Riley (1997).

title: Users can edit, regenerate, stop and undo AI actions
statement: Provide stop generation, edit prompt, regenerate, and undo for AI-applied changes; require confirmation before AI takes consequential actions.
rationale: Maps to: HAX G8–G9. Supports efficient correction and dismissal; keeps humans in control.

title: Collect granular feedback on AI output
statement: Offer lightweight feedback (thumbs, corrections) and explain how it is used.

title: Provide a path to a human
statement: Conversational agents offer an escape to human help, especially after repeated failure or for sensitive issues.
rationale: Maps to: User control. Users trapped with bots become frustrated.

title: Preserve conversation context
statement: The agent remembers context within a session (and across sessions where appropriate and disclosed), so users do not repeat themselves.
rationale: Maps to: HAX G12. Repetition is a top complaint about chatbots.
audit_check: Does the agent maintain context across turns?

title: Voice prompts are short with few options
statement: Keep spoken prompts brief, offer about three options at a time, put the most important information last, allow barge-in, and confirm critical inputs.
rationale: Maps to: Working memory. Audio is linear and taxes working memory.

title: Tables are scannable and accessible
statement: Use proper header cells, right-align numbers, keep headers visible on scroll, allow sorting where useful, and avoid tables for layout.
rationale: Maps to: WCAG 1.3.1. Supports comparison and screen readers.

title: Charts represent data honestly
statement: Bar charts start at zero; axes are labeled; scales are consistent across compared charts; avoid 3D and dual axes that mislead.
rationale: Maps to: Tufte. Misleading charts distort decisions (lie factor).

title: Label data directly and use accessible palettes
statement: Prefer direct labels over legends, use color-blind-safe palettes, and provide data tables or text alternatives.
rationale: Maps to: WCAG 1.4.1. Reduces split attention and supports color-blind and screen reader users.
audit_check: Are charts directly labeled, color-blind safe, and accompanied by text alternatives?

title: Dashboards answer the key question at a glance
statement: Lead with the few most important metrics, show comparison/context (targets, trends), and allow drill-down.
rationale: Maps to: Endsley SA. Situation awareness requires perception, comprehension and projection.

title: Meet Core Web Vitals
statement: LCP ≤ 2.5 s, INP ≤ 200 ms, CLS ≤ 0.1 at the 75th percentile.
rationale: Maps to: Nielsen #1. Slow pages lose users; Google uses CWV as a ranking signal.

title: Optimize perceived performance
statement: Show content progressively (skeletons, above-the-fold first), use optimistic updates for low-risk actions, and avoid blank screens.
rationale: Maps to: Nielsen #1. Perceived speed matters as much as measured speed.
audit_check: Does the UI render useful content progressively instead of a blank screen?

title: Optimize images and media
statement: Serve responsive, compressed images in modern formats, lazy-load below-the-fold media, and avoid autoplaying heavy video.
rationale: Maps to: Nielsen #1. Heavy pages are slow on mobile networks and cost users data.
audit_check: Are images responsive, compressed and lazy-loaded?
citation: Google Lighthouse audits; web.dev image guidance.

title: Language selector is findable and uses native names
statement: Show languages in their own names (e.g., "Español"), not flags, in a consistent location.
rationale: Maps to: Nielsen #2. Flags represent countries, not languages.
audit_check: Is the language switcher easy to find and labeled with native language names?

title: Layouts handle text expansion and RTL
statement: Allow labels and buttons to grow (30–40%+), avoid text in images, and mirror layouts for right-to-left languages.
rationale: Maps to: i18n. Fixed widths truncate translations.

title: Motion is purposeful and brief
statement: Use animation to show relationships, state changes and continuity, with short durations (~100–500 ms) and easing; never block interaction with animation.

title: No autoplaying audio/video with sound
statement: Media does not autoplay with sound; moving content can be paused.

title: Minimize steps to complete top tasks
statement: Remove unnecessary steps, pages, clicks and decisions from top tasks; each step must be a clear, mindless choice.

title: No dead ends
statement: Every screen offers a clear next step or way back; confirmation and error pages include onward links.
rationale: Maps to: Nielsen #3. Dead ends stall users and increase abandonment.

title: The next step is always clear
statement: On each screen, the primary next action is obvious and labeled with what it does.
rationale: Maps to: Cognitive walkthrough. Unclear next steps cause hesitation and drop-off.

title: Avoid forcing users across channels or platforms
statement: Users can complete a task in one place without being sent to multiple platforms, PDFs or phone calls without guidance.

statement: Allow saving progress and resuming later (with clear instructions) for long applications and setups.

statement: Signup requests only essential fields (often just email and password or SSO), deferring profile details.
